resources.string: Pick a photo, then corrupt its JPEG bytes.
%1$d quantizer byte(s) changed - the preview shows the result
Moves the average of every 8x8 block: the picture gets brighter or darker.
Moves the average colour of every block: colours pull apart or wash together.
Horizontal bands, in colour only (chroma table).
Vertical bands, in colour only (chroma table).
Squares in both directions: a checkerboard when u equals v, a plaid when they differ.
Squares in both directions, in colour only (chroma table).
Fine patterns need detail in the photo: on a smooth image the finest rows change nothing.
One number for every block. Turn the wheel or tap the arrows to step it one at a time.
Block average - moves the whole picture

JPEG does not store pixels. It splits the photo into 8x8 blocks, describes each block with 64 numbers, and the quantization tables (DQT) say how roughly each of those numbers is kept. Editing them changes how the photo is stored, not what was photographed.
The 64 DCT basis patterns of an 8x8 block

Every square below is one of those 64 numbers, drawn as the pattern it adds to each block: how much it wiggles, and in which direction. The top-left is flat, so it only moves the block\'s average. The further right and down, the finer the detail it carries.
Left to right: u counts wiggles across a block, from 0 to 7. Top to bottom: v counts them down the block.
Which square belongs to which button
The flip screen sorts those squares into four families. The outlined squares are the ones a family covers:
Each family exists twice: the luma table (drawn here) and the chroma table, whose buttons carry the word colour. The colour families tint the picture instead of adding brightness detail.
Each number is divided by its quantizer when the file is written and multiplied back when it is read, so a bigger quantizer keeps less of that pattern:
kept finely - the pattern stays smooth
kept roughly - the pattern flattens into bands
A quantizer is one byte, so it holds 0 to 255. Flipping bit k adds or removes 2 to the power k, which is why the high bits move the picture far more than the low ones:
The slider on the flip screen is the same thing, made continuous: left is a smaller quantizer (smoother there), right is larger (coarser, so that pattern rings).
The first byte of each table is not a quantizer - the flips that touch it make the file undecodable, so the flip screen leaves it out.
A pattern only shows where the photo has detail at that frequency. On a smooth photo the finest squares change nothing.
Colour families live in the second table, so the same pattern tints the picture rather than adding luma texture.

JPEG does not store pixels. It cuts the picture into squares of 8 by 8 pixels and writes 64 numbers for each square - how bright, and how the brightness wiggles inside it. Every glitch the app makes lands inside those squares, so they are also the shape of what you see when a file is corrupted.
one 8x8 square, shown large: 64 pixels, 64 numbers

A square is always 8 pixels, so the smaller the picture, the larger a share of it each square covers. Retuning the quantization table changes how much of each square is kept, and with fewer, bigger squares the result of that is far plainer: the same wiggle spreads across more of the frame instead of hiding in fine detail.
800 px wide - 8x8 squares are 1/100 of the width
3200 px wide - the same squares, 1/400 of the width

Every edit is applied to the whole file and decoded again to show you the result, so the work is proportional to the number of squares. Halving the width and the height leaves a quarter of the squares - and a quarter of the work:
Same scale for all three bars. The smaller file also saves and shares faster, and is easier to keep in memory while glitching.

The slider picks the width the file is saved at, and the button under it does the resize. Crop to 9:16 trims the sides, which removes squares again. Skip leaves the file at full size: the most faithful result, but the slowest to work with and the hardest to see anything in.
Couldn\'t decode this JPEG - go back and pick another image.
No usable bit found in %1$d tries - image unchanged. Keep pressing or reset.
Storage permission is needed to export.
area control needs a readable frame header
%1$d bytes here are skipped: every bit flip in them makes the file undecodable.
Damage now stops at window edges: each glitch is confined to a %1$d%% tall band.

Preview of the Huffman table edit
%1$d edits that were not a wreck
From your own sweep of b, e, f and g at 1080 px. Another photo may behave differently.

Tap to keep an edit, hold to see it first.
These tables are not the ones your sweep measured, so there is nothing classified to suggest. The exact values below still work.
Values you pick by hand are not classified: nothing measured them, so they may do nothing or wreck the picture.
Every code of every table, over the whole byte. Use this to reach a value that is not one bit away from the file\'s own.

Peeking - let go to put it back
The frame header could not be read, so code usage is unknown.

This file already carries restart markers, so code usage is unknown.
This file declares no Huffman tables to edit.
The scan data could not be walked, so code usage is unknown.
The code book behind the picture

JPEG does not store coefficients as numbers. For every 8x8 block it writes a string of Huffman codes, and each code stands for a symbol that says how far along the block to jump and how many bits the value needs. The Huffman tables are the dictionary those codes are read with: the quantization tables say how roughly the picture was kept, these say how it was written down.
A table in the file is a header, then a list of symbols. The header names the table and gives the length of every code; the list says what each code means, in code order.
Sixteen counts: how many codes of each length
The symbols, in code order - the only part this screen edits

Every bit of the name byte and of the sixteen counts makes the file undecodable, so this screen never offers them: the decoder reads as many symbols as the counts ask for, and a flip in a count breaks that agreement with the list that follows.
Most of this region is a trap

Of the 3328 bits in these tables, 630 make the file stop decoding, 1856 change nothing at all, and 631 wreck the picture on the sample photos. Only 211 are edits worth having. That is why this screen does not offer the tables themselves: it offers the 211, sorted by how much of a picture they changed.
The whole region in proportion, from your sweep.

They are not a guess. Your own sweep flipped every one of these bits in four sample photos and filed the result, and this screen reads that classification: an edit is offered when its sample was filed as something other than a wreck, and the heading it appears under is how many of the four photos it changed.

The four photos were b, e, f and g at 1080 px. A code that was a wreck there can be the one that looks best on a different picture, which is why the wrecked folder is still one tap away rather than deleted - and why the exact-value editor exists, with a warning that nothing measured what you set there.

Two things are filtered out of the list. Edits whose code this photo never emits cannot change anything, so they are hidden. And nothing that was filed as a wreck is shown until the wrecked filter is switched on.
A code is as loud as it is short

Codes are handed out by frequency: the shortest code goes to the pair of values the picture produces most often. That is why the codes at the top of the list are the ones an edit reaches furthest with - and why the screen keeps them behind their own heading rather than leading with them.
Every code of the luma detail table. The tall bright bars on the left are short codes, used constantly; the flat tail is 125 codes these photos never emit.
What a code can be changed to

In the detail tables a symbol packs two numbers into one byte: how many zero coefficients to skip, and how many bits the next value needs. Rather than exposing that byte, the screen offers the handful of meanings worth having - end the block, sixteen zeros, one more or less bit of value, one more or less skip - because only those few of the 256 possible values say anything you can picture.
Skip a few, then one four-bit value: the common case, and the one this code was designed for.
Skip nine, then one two-bit value: the same code, told to jump much further along the block.

Two of these symbols do something special. A skip of 0 with a size of 0 ends the block; a skip of 15 with a size of 0 means sixteen zeros in a row. Tap a choice to keep it, or hold it to see the picture before you commit.

In the two level tables the symbol is not a pair but a single number: how many bits the block level takes. The decoder reads exactly that many bits after every code, so changing one of these symbols puts the whole rest of the scan out of step - which is why they hit the picture far harder than a detail edit of the same size.
Two kinds of edit are left out entirely, because no picture comes out of them.
Every bit of a code length count. A changed count either overruns the table or leaves bytes over that the decoder then reads as the next table.
A level symbol of 16 or more. A block level cannot need more bits than the sample size, and past 15 the decoder stops on the stream.

Most of a table is usually dead weight. On the four sample photos only 77 of the luma detail table\'s 162 codes are ever emitted, and 45 of the colour detail table\'s - so most of the available edits cannot change anything on that photo. This screen counts that per image and hides the dead ones.

A code being used is not the same as a visible change. Skipping one more coefficient, or reading one bit more, can land inside what the encoder already rounded away - two thirds of the sample batch measured as no visible change at all.
Detail edits in the colour table register in the colour channels rather than the brightness; the level tables move brightness on the luma side and colour on the chroma side.
